title: How do software (SaaS) companies make money, and what matters in their cases?
description: Subscription software economics for case interviews: ARR, churn, net revenue retention, CAC and LTV, with a worked customer lifetime value.
hook: Software-as-a-service businesses are now common in cases, especially in tech and private equity interviews. Their economics revolve around recurring revenue: win a customer once, keep them for years, and sell them more over time.
body:
The measures that matter

  • ARR (annual recurring revenue): the yearly value of all active subscriptions.
  • Churn: the share of customers who cancel.
  • Net revenue retention: what last year's customers pay this year, after cancellations, downgrades and upgrades.
  • CAC (customer acquisition cost) and LTV (lifetime value).

A worked example: is growth healthy?

A customer pays £100 a month at an 80% gross margin, so £80 a month of profit. Monthly churn is 2.5%, so customers stay about 40 months on average (1 ÷ 0.025). LTV ≈ £80 × 40 = £3,200. If winning a customer costs £1,200, LTV is about 2.7 times CAC, slightly below the common rule of thumb of 3. Cutting churn to 2% would lift lifetime to 50 months and LTV to £4,000.

Why retention matters so much

Net revenue retention above 100% means existing customers grow on their own, through upgrades and extra seats, even before any new sales.

Typical SaaS case questions

  • Why is churn rising?
  • Should we add a free plan? (a freemium question)
  • How should we price a new product tier?
  • Is this company a good private equity investment?

Build a subscription business from its customer movements

Start with 1,000 customers paying £1,000 annually, or £1 million of annual recurring revenue (ARR). During the year, 80 customers cancel, 100 new customers join, and existing customers expand their contracts by £120,000. Assuming all customers are annual and the new customers pay the same amount, ending ARR is £1 million − £80,000 + £100,000 + £120,000 = £1.14 million. The company grew, but you need the components to understand how.

Gross revenue retention measures how much starting ARR remains after cancellations and contractions, excluding expansion. Here, with no downsells, it is 92%. Net revenue retention includes expansion from the starting cohort: (£1 million − £80,000 + £120,000) ÷ £1 million = 104%. New customer ARR belongs in neither of these retention numerators.

Now examine acquisition economics. If the company spends £600,000 on sales and marketing to win 100 new customers, its customer acquisition cost is £6,000. At £1,000 ARR and 80% gross margin, each customer contributes roughly £800 per full year before acquisition expenses; a rough gross-margin CAC payback is 7.5 years absent expansion or upfront collection benefits. That signals a problem even if ARR is growing. Real models should use customer cohorts, monthly timing and fully loaded acquisition costs.

In an interview, ask whether growth is driven by new logos, contract expansion or price increases, and whether customers remain long enough for acquisition spending to pay back. Avoid mistaking ARR for recognised revenue or cash collected.
